Temperature

 Home Physics Branches of physics Statistical physics Thermodynamics
OurBigBook.com Words: 8k Articles: 50
Temperature labels thermal equilibrium: two internally equilibrated bodies have the same temperature when contact permitting only heat exchange produces no net heat transfer. The zeroth law of thermodynamics makes the comparison transitive. If bodies A and B separately reach thermal equilibrium with the same thermometer without appreciably disturbing either body, they agree with each other. This is what lets a gas thermometer compare a metal block with water, despite their different internal energies and heat capacities. Insulation alone makes no such comparison: it can prevent heat transfer between bodies at different temperatures. [ref]
The zeroth law of thermodynamics establishes equality comparisons, but does not choose a numerical scale. Thermodynamic temperature supplies an absolute scale consistent with Carnot's theorem and entropy. For a simple compressible system at thermodynamic equilibrium with fixed particle number N and composition,
T=(∂S∂U​)V,N​,T1​=(∂U∂S​)V,N​.
(1)
Here U is internal energy, S is entropy, and V is volume; the second equality assumes the derivative can be inverted. Temperature is a thermodynamic conjugate variable to entropy and belongs to the intensive and extensive thermodynamic quantities as an intensive quantity. Its partial derivative tells us how much internal energy must change per unit change of entropy under the stated constraints. More general systems require their other mechanical and material variables to be held fixed too. [ref]
For an infinitesimal quantity δQ>0 of heat transferred from A to B, with no work or matter exchange, the equilibrium entropy changes give
dStotal​=δQ(TB​1​−TA​1​).
(2)
For ordinary positive temperatures, spontaneous heat transfer from TA​>TB​ increases total entropy; thermal equilibrium has TA​=TB​. This comparison uses changes in entropy, rather than the total internal energy contained in either body. A small hot object can have less internal energy than a large cool one. See entropy maximization under thermal contact for the equilibrium criterion and negative temperature for the special case of bounded energy spectra.
Express absolute thermodynamic temperature T in kelvin, and a Celsius reading tC​ in degree Celsius:
∘CtC​​=KT​−273.15,∘CΔtC​​=KΔT​.
(3)
The offset is exact: 300K corresponds to 26.85∘C, and 400K to 126.85∘C. Their absolute temperature ratio is 4/3; dividing their Celsius readings gives a different number. Thus gas thermometer pressure ratios and Carnot's theorem require thermodynamic temperature. The modern SI definition of the kelvin fixes the Boltzmann constant kB​=1.380649×10−23JK−1; a reference bath realizes or transfers the scale rather than defining that constant.[ref]
Temperature is not universally the mean kinetic energy of a particle. In a classical, nonrelativistic ideal gas at thermal equilibrium, the equipartition theorem gives the mean translational kinetic energy relative to the gas's bulk motion:
⟨21​m∣v−u∣2⟩=23​kB​T.
(4)
Here m is particle mass, v its velocity, and u the mean flow velocity. In this regime, different particle masses at the same temperature have equal mean translational kinetic energies but different characteristic speeds. A moving gas can also carry bulk kinetic energy without being hotter in its rest frame. Internal molecular modes and quantum statistics require further care; the equipartition theorem has classical assumptions, whereas the equilibrium entropy definition applies more widely. [ref]

Mean temperature (T=τ−1∫0τ​T(t)dt)

Words: 49
Temperature measurement OurBigBook.com
An average of a specified temperature record over a stated interval or ensemble. For a time mean, observations must represent elapsed durations: irregularly spaced readings generally require time weighting. The half-sum of a daily maximum and minimum is a conventional daily statistic and need not equal the continuous time mean.

An instrument for estimating high temperatures. The physical response and calibration must be specified; thermal expansion, a calorimetric transfer, electrical properties and emitted radiation lead to different methods and different limitations.

The temperature within soil or rock beneath the ground surface. Its time dependence can be governed by thermal conduction, fluid transport and internal heating; a homogeneous conduction-only approximation gives a heat equation.

Kinetic temperature (Tk​)

Words: 55
Temperature OurBigBook.com
For an isotropic nonrelativistic Maxwellian particle population, kinetic temperature describes random translational motion, with mean kinetic energy 3kB​Tk​/2 per particle after subtracting bulk motion. Different species can have different kinetic temperatures outside thermal equilibrium. A rotational excitation temperature equals the kinetic temperature only when the excitation is sufficiently thermalized; a radiation brightness temperature is another distinct quantity.

Electron temperature (Te​)

Words: 32
Temperature OurBigBook.com
The temperature parameter describing a thermal electron velocity distribution. Electron-impact excitation coefficients depend on it through both the speed distribution and excitation thresholds. In a dilute plasma, electron and ion temperatures need not coincide.

Absolute zero (0K)

Words: 43
Temperature OurBigBook.com
Absolute zero is the zero of thermodynamic temperature, corresponding to −273.15∘C. For a system with a nondegenerate ground state, equilibrium entropy approaches zero as temperature approaches absolute zero. This does not mean that every quantum degree of freedom loses its zero-point energy. The entropy statement and the operational unattainability of absolute zero require their respective physical assumptions.

Adiabatic demagnetization

Words: 2k Articles: 9
Temperature OurBigBook.com
A cooling method that reduces an applied magnetic field while suppressing heat transfer to or from the material. For a suitable material exhibiting paramagnetism, an approximately reversible field reduction can lower its temperature at approximately constant entropy.
The preparation matters as much as the field reduction. First establish thermal equilibrium with a cold heat bath, then raise the magnetic field while maintaining the bath temperature: this is magnetization in an isothermal process. The bath accepts heat and the material loses magnetic entropy. Next open a heat switch, thermally isolating the working material, and lower the magnetic field. If the sweep maintains internal thermal equilibrium with negligible entropy production, this second leg is an isentropic process. An adiabatic process alone does not guarantee constant entropy.
The attraction is a controllable energy scale: changing the magnetic field changes the separation of magnetic energy levels, even across a thermally insulating gap. This lets an already cold solid become colder without needing a colder contacting heat bath. A practical refrigerator also needs a load, a period of absorbing its heat, and a reset that rejects accumulated entropy to the bath. A single field sweep has finite cooling capacity.

Demagnetization with a linear-heat-capacity load (Tf​=Ti​−(Nθ/M)Δsmag​/kB​)

Words: 76
Adiabatic demagnetization OurBigBook.com
Let N independent spin-J moments and a load with heat capacity CL​=MkB​T/θ remain in equilibrium during reversible isolated demagnetization. Then SL​(T)=SL​(0)+MkB​T/θ. Fully removing the field raises each spin entropy by its initial magnetic entropy deficit. Total entropy conservation gives NΔsmag​=MkB​(Ti​−Tf​)/θ, yielding the title result. The formula assumes positive final temperature, validity of the load law throughout the interval, negligible additional entropy contributions and an attainable equilibrated low-field endpoint. Interactions require an actual many-body entropy instead of the independent-spin expression.

Magnetic-entropy demagnetization adiabat

Words: 33
Adiabatic demagnetization OurBigBook.com
When the entropy of independent magnetic moments dominates, a reversible isolated change fixes B/T. Lowering the field therefore lowers temperature as Tf​/Ti​=Bf​/Bi​. Other heat capacities, internal interactions and residual fields limit this ideal relation.

Magnetic entropy (Smag​)

Words: 943 Articles: 4
Adiabatic demagnetization OurBigBook.com
Magnetic entropy counts the uncertainty in the occupied magnetic microstates. For independent localized magnetic moments with one-site probabilities pj​,
Smag​=−NkB​∑j​pj​lnpj​,
(5)
where N counts sites and kB​ is the Boltzmann constant. This is the Gibbs entropy for the magnetic degrees of freedom. Equal occupation of two states gives NkB​ln2; certain occupation of one state gives zero. Calling this disorder is useful only if the relevant states and their probabilities are specified. In an interacting material, correlations generally prevent replacing the many-body Gibbs entropy by this sum of independent one-site contributions.
Increasing the magnetic field at fixed positive temperature favors lower magnetic energy levels, reducing magnetic entropy. During ideal isolated demagnetization, both the level separation and temperature fall together, leaving the occupation probabilities unchanged. Thus the independent-spin idealization cools without increasing spin disorder along the isolated leg. When a real crystal's vibrating lattice also cools, its lost entropy can instead be taken up by the magnetic degrees of freedom. The conserved quantity is the total entropy of the thermally isolated stage, including any attached load in thermal equilibrium.

Magnetic entropy deficit (Δsmag​=smax​−s(T,B))

Words: 56
Magnetic entropy OurBigBook.com
The magnetic entropy deficit is the entropy increase still available to independent moments as their field polarization is removed. For a spin-J multiplet, smax​=kB​ln(2J+1) and the high-temperature deficit is kB​J(J+1)[gμB​B/(kB​T)]2/6. Isothermal magnetization creates this deficit while rejecting heat to a bath. Subsequent reversible demagnetization can absorb entropy from a cooling load. The deficit, not the initial absolute magnetic entropy, measures that capacity.

Entropy of a finite magnetic multiplet (sJ​/kB​=lnZJ​−x∂x​lnZJ​)

Words: 55
Magnetic entropy OurBigBook.com
For magnetic quantum numbers m=−J,…,J, energies Em​=−mgμB​B and x=gμB​B/(kB​T), the partition function is ZJ​=∑m​emx=sinh[(2J+1)x/2]/sinh(x/2). Its entropy is the title expression, a function of B/T alone. At small J∣x∣, sJ​/kB​=ln(2J+1)−J(J+1)x2/6+O(x4). The maximal entropy is kB​ln(2J+1) at zero splitting. A fixed independent-spin entropy consequently fixes B/T; an attached heat load changes the combined isentropic path.

Two-level paramagnetic cooling model (x=μB/(kB​T))

Words: 672 Articles: 1
Magnetic entropy OurBigBook.com
Use the independent spin-one-half two-level system with fixed N distinguishable sites and Hamiltonian levels E±​=±μB, where μ>0 is the magnitude of the field-axis magnetic moment and B>0 is a uniform externally controlled magnetic field. Assume positive temperature, no interactions between sites, and no appreciable lattice or load entropy. The two levels differ by 2μB. With inverse temperature β, the canonical ensemble gives the one-site and total partition functions
β=kB​T1​,x=βμB,z=ex+e−x=2coshx,Z=zN,p−​=2coshxex​,p+​=2coshxe−x​.
(6)
Here the minus subscript denotes the lower energy −μB. Factorization of the partition function requires additive energy and independent sites; there is no particle-exchange factor N! for these fixed distinguishable sites.
Differentiate the partition function, holding B fixed when differentiating with respect to β. The internal energy, Helmholtz free energy, total field-axis magnetic moment m, and magnetic entropy are
Umag​=−∂β​lnZ=−NμBtanhx,F=−NkB​Tln(2coshx),
(7)
m=−(∂B∂F​)T​=Nμtanhx,NkB​Smag​​=NlnZ+βUmag​​=ln(2coshx)−xtanhx=:s(x).
(8)
The extensive moment m is distinct from magnetization, the moment per unit volume. Direct substitution of p±​ into the Gibbs entropy gives the same s(x) independently of the free-energy derivative.
At fixed B, the magnetic heat capacity is
CB,mag​=(∂T∂Umag​​)B​=NkB​x2sech2x≥0,dxds​=−xsech2x<0(x>0).
(9)
Strict decrease makes s invertible on x>0. Constant magnetic entropy therefore fixes x, not B or T separately:
TB​=constant,Ti​Tf​​=Bi​Bf​​(Bi​,Bf​,Ti​,Tf​>0).
(10)
The partition function may be used to label these equilibrium states even though the isolated cooling leg has no external heat bath. Actual thermalization of the lattice and load additionally requires a sufficiently fast spin-lattice relaxation; perfectly uncoupled spins by themselves cannot refrigerate an attached object.
The limiting cases are instructive. For x≪1, s(x)=ln2−x2/2+O(x4), m≃Nμ2B/(kB​T), and CB,mag​≃NkB​x2. The moment response reproduces Curie's law. For x≫1, s(x)≃(1+2x)e−2x and the upper-state occupation is exponentially small. Taking B→0 at fixed T>0 gives s→ln2; taking T→0 at fixed B>0 gives s→0. The origin has a path-dependent limit. Extrapolating a line of constant x to B=T=0 does not construct a usable zero-temperature state or prove that a real material retains independent degenerate spins there.
Constant-entropy magnetic cooling example (Tf​=Ti​Bf​/Bi​)
Words: 346
Two-level paramagnetic cooling model OurBigBook.com
Choose a fictional two-level refrigerant with μ/kB​=1KT−1, where the upright T denotes tesla. This chosen moment is a convenient model parameter, not a fitted property of the historical salt. At bath temperature Tb​=1K, raise B from 0.20T to 1.00T. Then x increases from 0.20 to 1.00, so
s(0.20)=0.673540…,s(1)=0.365334…,NkB​Tb​Qin​​=s(1)−s(0.20)=−0.308206….
(11)
The last equality assumes a reversible isothermal process of magnetization; negative Qin​ means the refrigerant rejects heat. The bath gains 0.308206…NkB​ of entropy, balancing the stage's loss in this reversible limit. An appreciable temperature difference during real heat transfer adds entropy production.
Now open the heat switch and reduce B from 1.00T to 0.10T. Constant x=1 gives Tf​=0.10K. Throughout this ideal cooling leg, p−​=0.880797…, p+​=0.119203…, and Smag​=0.365334…NkB​. Neither state becomes more probable. Field reduction shrinks the energy gap by ten while preserving the Boltzmann distribution's dimensionless ratio of gap to temperature.
There is a subtle energy check. For the spin Hamiltonian convention used here, external-field interaction energy belongs to Umag​, so reversible work done on the spin subsystem is δWon​=−mdB and
dUmag​=TdSmag​−mdB.
(12)
On the isolated leg, Q=0 but Umag​ increases from −0.761594…NkB​K to −0.0761594…NkB​K, becoming less negative as the gap shrinks. Integrating −mdB at constant x=1 supplies exactly +0.685435…NkB​K. Cooling therefore need not decrease this chosen spin internal energy. An account of work exchanged with a magnet circuit must specify where field interaction energy is assigned before comparing signs. The occupation ratio and temperature prediction do not depend on that bookkeeping choice.
For the isothermal preparation, direct integration gives Won​/(NkB​Tb​)=−ln[cosh(1)/cosh(0.20)]=−0.413913…. The endpoint internal energy difference is −0.722119…NkB​Tb​, equal to Qin​+Won​. This independently checks both the rejected heat and the magnetic-work sign in the chosen convention.

Giauque-MacDougall magnetic cooling experiment (1933)

Words: 184
Adiabatic demagnetization OurBigBook.com
William Francis Giauque's 1949 lecture, Some Consequences of Low Temperature Research in Chemical Thermodynamics, credits Peter Debye with an independent proposal. It describes gadolinium sulfate octahydrate in a jacket immersed in liquid helium, with an external solenoid. Exchange gas conducts away heat during magnetization; evacuation isolates the sample before field reduction. A liquid-nitrogen shield reduces radiative heat transfer. Its photograph identifies the 1933 apparatus operated with Duncan Peck MacDougall. An inductance bridge reads the sample's magnetic susceptibility; measuring coils remain outside the evacuated jacket in liquid helium. Increasing magnetic susceptibility indicates cooling, but converting it to temperature using Curie's law becomes approximate as that law fails.[ref]
The measurement logic deserves a separate check. A changed inductance alone is not an absolute temperature calibration: the sample geometry, applied measuring magnetic field, and constitutive response enter the inference. A modern control would compare the susceptibility-based thermometer with an independently calibrated thermometer over their common range, check recovery after repeated sweeps, and measure subsequent warming to bound incoming heat. These are proposed controls derived from the readout principle, rather than additional procedures attributed to the 1933 experiment. The historical working salt has a richer magnetic level structure than the illustrative two-level paramagnetic cooling model.

Limits of adiabatic demagnetization

Words: 343
Adiabatic demagnetization OurBigBook.com
Three distinct effects spoil indefinite T∝B cooling: extra entropy outside the spin subsystem, additional magnetic energy scales, and irreversible heat or work input. They can be distinguished with a thermodynamic derivative. For a smooth equilibrium Helmholtz free energy obeying dF=−SdT−mdB, a Maxwell relation gives
dS=TCB​​dT+(∂T∂m​)B​dB,(dBdT​)S​=−CB​T​(∂T∂m​)B​.
(13)
Here CB​ is the total heat capacity participating in the stage's thermal equilibrium. The ideal model has (∂m/∂T)B​=−CB,mag​/B. If its spins share temperature with a field-independent lattice and load of combined heat capacity Cother​>0, then
(dBdT​)Stotal​​=BT​CB,mag​+Cother​CB,mag​​.
(14)
The positive slope still means cooling when dB<0, but its smaller magnitude gives less cooling per fractional field reduction. For example, a low-temperature Debye model gives a lattice entropy proportional to T3. As that lattice entropy falls, the spins take up the released entropy; x can no longer remain constant. A weak enough coupling to neglect its equilibrium interaction energy can still be strong enough to exchange heat on the sweep timescale.
Interactions between magnetic moments, including exchange interaction and the fields of neighboring magnetic dipole moments, introduce energy scales that do not vanish with the applied B. Once they compete with kB​T or μB, the independent-site partition function fails. Correlations and possible magnetic ordering alter the available magnetic entropy and the cooling curve. Simply setting the external magnetic field to zero does not eliminate those interactions. Different refrigerants therefore need their own measured equilibrium properties; there is no universal final temperature from the applied-field ratio alone.
Finally, a real open heat switch has residual thermal conductance; supports, wires and radiation carry incoming heat. Field changes may also dissipate energy. Locally near thermal equilibrium, with incoming heat rate Q˙​leak​ and internal entropy production rate S˙prod​, the stage balance becomes
dtdS​=TQ˙​leak​​+S˙prod​,CB​T˙=−T(∂T∂m​)B​B˙+Q˙​leak​+TS˙prod​.
(15)
This uses a common stage temperature; a non-equilibrated load requires separate balances. The sweep must allow spin-lattice relaxation while remaining fast enough to limit accumulated parasitic heat. At fixed B, the same balance explains warming and finite hold time. Useful refrigeration is the controlled absorption of a load's heat during that finite interval, followed by a renewed isothermal process of magnetization to export its entropy.

International Temperature Scale of 1990 (T90​)

Words: 40
Temperature OurBigBook.com
The International Temperature Scale of 1990 is a practical scale for reproducible temperature measurements. Its assigned reference points and interpolation procedures approximate thermodynamic temperature. A calibrated standard platinum resistance thermometer transfers this scale over specified intervals; it does not define the modern kelvin.[ref]

Thermometer

Words: 3k Articles: 16
Temperature OurBigBook.com
A thermometer measures temperature through a physical response whose relation to temperature is known. Examples include the length change from thermal expansion, a change in electrical resistance, and the pressure of a gas thermometer. If the response function X=f(T) is an injective function over the working range, its measured value determines T=f−1(X) through the inverse function. Thermometer calibration establishes that relation for the particular instrument and measurement conditions. Two matching readings are meaningful only after calibration to a common scale and with the probes sampling comparable equilibrium states. [ref]
For a contact thermometer, the sensing part must reach thermal equilibrium with the region being measured. That region may differ from the rest of the object: an immersed probe near a heater can read a local temperature while the surrounding water remains cooler. A stable reading can also be a steady state set by competing heat transfer paths to the sample and the room. Good contact, adequate immersion, mixing where appropriate, and checks for spatial differences help establish which temperature the reading represents. These are measurement controls inferred from the thermal equilibrium requirement, not a guarantee that every flat trace is equilibrium.
A thermometer also changes the sample it touches. Consider an original toy calculation with an initially uniform sample at To​=350K, a probe at Tp​=300K, and constant whole-body heat capacities Co​=100JK−1 and Cp​=1JK−1. Suppose together they form an isolated system, with no work or phase transition and negligible contact energy. The first law of thermodynamics and thermal equilibrium give
Tf​=Co​+Cp​Co​To​+Cp​Tp​​=349.50495…K,Tf​−To​=Co​+Cp​Cp​​(Tp​−To​).
(16)
The final thermometer reading underestimates the sample's original temperature by about 0.495K, although it correctly measures their new common temperature. The disturbance becomes small when the participating probe heat capacity is small compared with the sample's. A large controlled heat bath is a different limit: it supplies or removes heat while approximately maintaining its own temperature.
Waiting time is a separate issue from disturbance. Under a toy Newton's law of cooling model for a uniform probe in a maintained heat bath, a constant contact conductance G gives
Cp​dtdTp​​=G(Tb​−Tp​),Tp​(t)=Tb​+[Tp​(0)−Tb​]e−t/τ,τ=GCp​​.
(17)
The time constant τ controls this exponential decay. For stipulated values Tb​=350K, Tp​(0)=300K and τ=5s, the probe reads about 331.61K after one time constant and 347.51K after three. These are calculated values, not an instrument specification or measured data. Real probes may have multiple relaxation times and additional heat transfer paths; choose an equilibration criterion from the required accuracy, rather than assuming that a fixed waiting time works universally.

A bulb-volume change shifts the indicated temperature. Contraction raises the liquid column at a fixed temperature; expansion lowers it. Permanent and temporary changes require distinction when interpreting an ice-point check.[ref]

Resistance thermometer

Thermometer OurBigBook.com
A thermometer that infers temperature from a calibrated electrical resistance. Measuring current can heat its sensing element; extrapolation toward zero current controls that bias in the saturation-pressure equilibrium measurement.

Platinum resistance thermometer

Words: 1k Articles: 6
Resistance thermometer OurBigBook.com
A resistance thermometer using platinum as its sensing material. It provides the temperature readout in the saturation-pressure equilibrium measurement.
Transduction turns electrical resistance into a temperature indication. A uniform wire has R=ρel​ℓ/A, with electrical resistivity ρel​, length ℓ, and cross-sectional area A. Stronger atomic vibrations at higher temperature scatter electrons more, increasing platinum's electrical resistivity; impurities and crystallographic defects also contribute.[ref]
A small known electric current I and measured electric potential difference V give R=V/I through Ohm's law; a resistance bridge can instead compare the element with a reference resistor. Inverting the calibrated response then gives the sensing element's temperature. This makes electrical readout convenient, but the platinum resistance thermometer lead resistance error, resistance thermometer self-heating, and resistance thermometer immersion test explain why a stable display alone is insufficient. The gas thermometer supplies a contrasting route through an equation of state; the saturation-pressure equilibrium measurement shows why a trustworthy independent temperature readout matters.
Standard platinum resistance thermometer
Words: 115
Platinum resistance thermometer OurBigBook.com
A standard platinum resistance thermometer uses very pure, annealed platinum with strain-limiting construction. An industrial platinum resistance thermometer commonly uses supported wire or a film. Their response curves differ.[ref]
The word standard describes the instrument's metrological role. Calibrated SPRTs realize specified interpolation intervals of the International Temperature Scale of 1990 and transfer reference temperatures to other thermometers.[ref] They are primary standards for realizing that practical scale, but their electrical resistance alone does not determine absolute thermodynamic temperature without calibration. Primary thermometry such as the corrected gas thermometer obtains thermodynamic temperature from a physical law. A reference in a comparison bath may be an SPRT; an individually calibrated industrial platinum resistance thermometer can also serve as a working reference with an appropriate uncertainty.
Industrial platinum resistance thermometer
Words: 344 Articles: 2
Platinum resistance thermometer OurBigBook.com
An industrial platinum resistance thermometer is a platinum resistance thermometer built for practical measurement conditions. The label Pt100 specifies a nominal reference electrical resistance, not an SPRT, a calibration certificate, or a universal accuracy. Calibrate the probe together with its readout when the desired result is the performance of the complete indicating system.
Pt100 (R0​=100Ω)
Words: 300 Articles: 1
Industrial platinum resistance thermometer OurBigBook.com
A Pt100 has nominal electrical resistance 100Ω at 0∘C.[ref] Here 0∘C is the reference for the nominal element designation; it is distinct from the 0.01∘C water triple point used in SPRT calibration. The following Pt100 local linear model deliberately stipulates one approximate response for calculations.
Pt100 local linear model (R=R0​(1+αt))
Words: 250
Pt100 OurBigBook.com
Choose the illustrative local model
R(t)=R0​(1+αt),R0​=100Ω,α=0.00385(∘C)−1.
(18)
Here t is the Celsius temperature, measured relative to 0∘C, so αt is dimensionless. For this chosen affine function, the derivative and inverse relation are
dtdR​=R0​α=0.385Ω/∘C,t=αR/R0​−1​,Δt=0.385Ω/∘CΔR​.
(19)
Calculated values are R(0∘C)=100Ω, R(20∘C)=107.70Ω, R(25∘C)=109.625Ω, and R(50∘C)=119.25Ω. These are model outputs, not measurements or an assertion that any real Pt100 follows this line exactly. The number 0.00385 here is the chosen slope parameter; it is not a universal local derivative for all platinum resistance thermometers. Curvature, manufacturing differences, and the fitted calibration interval matter. A wider-range calibration uses a validated response curve rather than extrapolating this line indefinitely.
For a separate synthetic thermometer calibration, stipulate Ra​=100.20Ω at ta​=0∘C and Rb​=119.60Ω at tb​=50∘C. A two-point affine function has slope 0.388Ω/∘C and gives
t=0.388Ω/∘CR−100.20Ω​.
(20)
Thus R=109.90Ω would indicate 25∘C. If an additional synthetic check at reference 25∘C instead supplied 110.10Ω, the line would indicate 25.515…∘C. The 0.20Ω residual exposes disagreement that two fitted points cannot reveal. This separate example changes both offset and slope; it is not a replacement specification for the nominal Pt100 local linear model.
Platinum resistance thermometer comparison calibration
Words: 246
Platinum resistance thermometer OurBigBook.com
A 1998 NIST account describes stirred comparison baths, a reference SPRT with a 30 Hz resistance bridge, and a temperature-controlled 100Ω reference resistor. The test IPRTs used a 1mA current source, a scanner, and an 8½-digit voltmeter. Separate current and voltage leads made each test probe a four-terminal device; readings in both current directions supplied voltage ratios to the reference resistor.[ref]
Its program bracketed test readings with reference SPRT readings and repeated a block if bath drift was excessive. A check SPRT monitored the system; reference water-triple point measurements checked stability. Sensor depths were matched, and unfamiliar probes underwent immersion tests. Ice and water-triple point readings before and after calibration checked changes. Additional points could test the fitted curve. Reported calibration uncertainties excluded transport, subsequent drift, hysteresis, and the user's measurement system. These are controls and limits of that documented apparatus, not an accuracy promise for all platinum resistance thermometers.[ref]
The inference is a pair: reference temperature from the SPRT, test electrical resistance from the electrical readout. Record measuring electric current, wiring, immersion, and the stated reference scale with each pair. A bath controller's setpoint is not itself the calibrated reference temperature. A pressure ratio cancels the unknown gas inventory and bulb size in the ideal constant-volume limit. This cancellation is the method's appeal: a mechanical measurement transfers an absolute temperature scale between different materials. The Maxwell speed distribution and ideal gas pressure from wall collisions explain the microscopic origin of the response. [ref]
For an original ideal-model calculation, choose T0​=300K, P0​=120kPa and P=160kPa. Then T=400K. These are stipulated values, not observations. Both pressures must be absolute, referred to vacuum. If the surrounding atmospheric pressure were 100kPa, the corresponding gauge pressures would be 20 and 60kPa; their ratio is three, which would incorrectly predict 900K. A pressure difference from the atmosphere cannot be substituted into the ideal gas law.
A motivating calibration experiment. Schooley's account of the NBS/NIST work describes a helium-filled metal bulb, a capillary, a capacitance diaphragm gauge, and a mercury pressure standard. Circulating bath liquid passed the bulb assembly and platinum resistance thermometers. The resistance probes checked the surrounding temperature; gas pressure supplied the independent thermodynamic comparison. In an early series, workers filled the cleaned bulb with purified helium at the highest test temperature, checked pressure over three hours, then measured at lower temperatures and near a reference at 0∘C. Six filling pressures allowed extrapolation toward zero pressure. [ref]
To turn this principle into a readable measurement protocol, use the following controls. These steps are a proposed teaching interpretation of the cited apparatus, rather than additional reported NBS observations:
  • Define the inventory. Evacuate and clean the bulb and connecting tube, fill with a known pure gas, close the filling valve, and keep the same total particle number during each reference/test comparison. Monitor pressure at a maintained temperature before and after a run. A leak changes N; a slow drift can also reflect contamination, sorption, or imperfect equilibration, so pressure stability alone does not identify its cause.
  • Measure the reference. Place the bulb in a controlled environment with independently assigned T0​. Record P0​ after thermalization, together with the independent thermometer readings and their spread. A reference near 0∘C has an absolute temperature near 273.15K, rather than zero temperature. Repeating reference readings tests whether the inventory or apparatus changed during the comparison.
  • Measure the test state. Change the bath setting, allow the bulb and gas to settle, and record P only when the surrounding thermometers and pressure are sufficiently stable for the intended accuracy. Compare readings at different positions and vary the settling time. Record the connecting tube's temperature profile too: uniform bath temperature does not make the entire connecting tube isothermal.
  • Measure the volume changes. Determine the bulb's thermal expansion and its deformation from differences between inside and outside pressure. Measure the connecting tube's dimensions and the effective valve volume. “Constant volume” is the ideal model; a real vessel expands. These measurements supply corrections, even though the absolute bulb volume cancels in the simplest pressure ratio.
  • Measure pressure against a reference. For a liquid-column pressure standard, measure the vertical column height, the liquid's temperature-dependent mass density, local gravitational acceleration, and the reference-side pressure. Include diaphragm offsets and the gas's hydrostatic pressure change between the sensor and bulb. The pressure needed in the equation of state is at the bulb, not automatically at the remote gauge.
The corresponding NBS apparatus used a protective case with an outer helium layer held close to the bulb pressure, reducing pressure deformation while aiding thermal contact. Thermal expansion was measured on bulb material. Gas in the capillary remained partly outside the hot region, requiring a measured tube temperature profile and geometry. Pure working gas also mattered: contaminants that sorb on surfaces can change the freely circulating inventory. These are physical effects to measure or bound, rather than scatter that disappears by averaging. [ref]

If the bulb expands by 0.1% and Z=1 at both states, the toy pressure ratio above gives 400.4K, rather than 400K. Cryogenics

Words: 2k Articles: 10
Temperature OurBigBook.com
Cryogenics studies the production and use of very low temperatures. Its experimental challenge is a balance of rates: a refrigerator must remove energy from a cold region faster than unwanted heat transfer supplies it. A low temperature reading alone does not establish a useful cooling capacity. A maintained cold liquid bath is especially valuable because latent heat allows it to absorb heat while its phase fraction changes at nearly fixed temperature and pressure.
Helium liquefaction illustrates why staged cooling and recovery of a returning stream's cooling capacity matter. A counterflow heat exchanger transfers heat from the incoming stream to the colder returning stream without mixing them. This reduces the incoming specific enthalpy before expansion. The heat exchanger recovers cooling already produced; the surrounding refrigerator still requires input work and rejection of heat to a warmer environment.

Helium liquefaction converts helium gas into a collectable liquid. It creates a bath for investigating material properties at very low temperatures, including superconductivity. The central question is how the incoming specific enthalpy compares with the specific enthalpies of the outgoing liquid and vapor. The liquefaction enthalpy budget makes that comparison explicit; a temperature decrease by itself does not specify a liquid yield.
In a Joule-Thomson effect cooling stage, a throttling pressure drop approximately preserves enthalpy under the assumptions of the steady-flow energy balance. For an ideal gas, specific enthalpy depends only on temperature: with positive specific heat capacity at constant pressure, equal specific enthalpy means equal temperature. Thus its Joule-Thomson coefficient is zero. An ideal gas also supplies no liquid branch. Cooling by throttling depends on real gas properties; expansion is not an automatic source of refrigeration.
For a local drop dp<0, dT=μJT​dp cools only where the Joule-Thomson coefficient is positive. Precooling must bring the real gas into a useful cooling region, with enough cooling to overcome unwanted heat transfer. A finite expansion can cross a Joule-Thomson inversion curve; its final state requires the full enthalpy balance, including phase coexistence if liquid forms. Kamerlingh Onnes's 1908 helium liquefaction experiment combined external precooling with regeneration to reach that regime. The Joule-Thomson effect article develops the throttling identities and their assumptions.

On 10 July 1908, Heike Kamerlingh Onnes's Leiden laboratory circulated purified helium through liquid air and evaporatively cooled liquid-hydrogen precooling, a regenerative heat exchanger, and an expansion valve. Returning helium cooled incoming helium; liquid collected in a transparent vacuum vessel. Reflected light revealed its liquid meniscus, crossed by thermocouple wires. Subsequent mass density and spectroscopy checks tested contamination.[ref]
A constant-volume helium gas thermometer below the valve supplied the temperature indication. An oxygen boiling reference check disagreed with its expected reading; the real gas correction to thermodynamic temperature remained provisional. A temperature plateau suggested immersion before the liquid meniscus was recognized.[ref]
The measurement principles separate two questions. A visible liquid meniscus establishes an interface; a gas thermometer estimates temperature through an equation of state. A stationary temperature trace can also result from a steady state without phase coexistence, so it cannot replace the interface observation. Conversely, seeing a liquid does not calibrate a thermometer. Thermometer calibration, the gas thermometer dead-space correction, departures from the ideal gas law and incomplete thermal equilibrium all matter when assigning an absolute temperature. A check far from the intended measurement range tests the instrument but does not by itself bound every low-temperature error.

The inlet has mass flow rate m˙>0 and specific enthalpy hin​. The outlets are equilibrium liquid and vapor at one fixed pressure, with specific enthalpies hl​ and hg​. Assume steady flow, no shaft work, and negligible bulk kinetic energy and gravitational potential energy changes. The steady-flow energy balance gives
hin​+q=yhl​+(1−y)hg​,L=hg​−hl​>0,y=Lhg​−hin​−q​.

For a deliberately dimensionless example, choose
η=Lhin​−hl​​=0.70,ℓ=Lq​=0.05,y=1−η−ℓ=0.25.
(31)
Per unit incoming mass, one quarter leaves as liquid and three quarters as vapor. With zero incoming heat, the same inlet would give y=0.30. Increasing q/L to 0.20 reduces y to 0.10, and q/L=0.30 reaches the no-liquid boundary. These are chosen model values, not helium property data or a historical yield. In normalized enthalpy units with hl​=0 and hg​=1, conservation checks directly: 0.70+0.05=0.25×0+0.75×1.
The admissible interval is hl​≤hin​+q≤hg​, or 0≤y≤1. Outside it, the assumed equilibrium two-phase outlet fails: an enthalpy above hg​ requires a hotter single-vapor outlet under these assumptions, rather than a negative amount of liquid. Below hl​, a colder liquid or a different thermodynamic phase must be considered. The balance does not predict its own outlet pressure, temperature or helium property functions.
At fixed outlet pressure, hence fixed L, the derivatives are ∂y/∂hin​=−1/L and ∂y/∂q=−1/L. Lowering inlet specific enthalpy by regeneration and reducing incoming heat therefore buy the same increase in liquid mass fraction per unit energy per unit mass in this model. Adding any constant to all three specific enthalpies leaves y unchanged. This independence of the arbitrary enthalpy reference makes the balance useful even when property tables choose different zero points.

Efficient thermal conduction within each material does not guarantee efficient heat transfer between them. The solid–helium case is Kapitza resistance; the broader concept also includes solid–solid interfaces. [ref]

ΔT=Ts​−Tl​,Q˙​=Aq,rB​=qΔT​[Km2W−1],RB​=Q˙​ΔT​=ArB​​[KW−1].

At nonzero heat flux, the two sides are outside mutual thermal equilibrium. A measured difference between distant thermometers also contains bulk temperature gradients, which must be measured or bounded before assigning all of it to the interface.

dtdUint​​=Aqin​−Aqout​.
